verses.text: He came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed; but his father was a Greek.
The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him.
Paul wanted to have him go out with him, and he took and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts; for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered the decrees to them to keep which had been ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem.
So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily.
When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.
When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them.
Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas.
A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.
Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis;
and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony. We were staying some days in this city.
On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down, and spoke to the women who had come together.
A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us; whose heart the Lord opened to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.
When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay.” So she persuaded us.
As we were going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune telling.
Following Paul and us, she cried out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!”
She was doing this for many days. But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that very hour.
But when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas, and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers.
When they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city,
and advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.”
The multitude rose up together against them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off of them, and commanded them to be beaten with rods.
When they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely,
who, having received such a command, threw them into the inner prison, and secured their feet in the stocks.
But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.
The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!”
He called for lights, sprang in, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas,
brought them out, and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
They spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house.
He took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household.
He brought them up into his house, and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly, with all his household, having believed in God.
But when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, “Let those men go.”
The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go; now therefore come out, and go in peace.”

But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!”
The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans,
and they came and begged them. When they had brought them out, they asked them to depart from the city.
They went out of the prison, and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them, and departed.

footnotes.content: Timothy steps onto the stage here—a young man caught between two worlds, Jewish mother and Greek father. Paul saw in him the makings of a faithful shepherd, the kind who could bridge that divide with grace. Sometimes the Lord plants us right where our heritage teaches us to listen to both sides.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers at Lystra and Iconium had watched Timothy already, and their testimony was good. What a mercy, to be known well by those who walk near you. A faithful reputation starts in secret, when nobody's watching but the ones who share your pew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul circumcised Timothy not out of fear, but out of love—the Jews in those parts knew his Greek father, and Paul wanted no stumbling block to Timothy's ministry. Sometimes obedience means meeting people where their conscience stands, not where ours does.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul carried the decrees from Jerusalem like a mailman carrying peace. The apostles and elders had settled hard questions in council; now Paul spreads that settled mind through the cities. There's steadiness in following what wise ones have already worked through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Strengthened in faith, and numbers grew. I've always loved this rhythm—when the deep things of God take root, people multiply around them. Growth that sticks is always from the inside out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Holy Spirit said no to Asia, a wealthy Roman province that should have seemed the obvious door. But the Spirit's map is not the world's map. Sometimes the greatest gift is not permission but redirection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bithynia tempted them next—another closing door. Paul and Silas had to learn that obedience often looks like a series of gentle no's, each one nudging them toward a yes they hadn't yet seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They came to Troas, a port city where three roads met. Troas felt like a dead end—nowhere left to go. But dead ends are where God often whispers most clearly to those willing to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Macedonian call came in the night, a man's face in a dream—"Come help us." This is how the gospel reached Europe. One vision, one open heart willing to follow a voice in the dark, and the path of centuries turned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the shift: "we" suddenly appears in the text—Luke joins them here. The company had grown, and with it, a new sense of shared calling. The Lord often draws us forward not alone but in company.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Troas to Samothrace to Neapolis—three ports in two days' sailing. They didn't know what waited for them. We're watching the gospel literally cross water into new lands, carried by men who simply said yes to a dream.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philippi, a Roman colony, foremost of the district—not a Jewish center, but a gentile city. They stayed awhile, settling in to listen and watch and wait for where the Lord would open a heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Sabbath by the riverside—no synagogue in Philippi, so believers gathered outside the city by the water. I think of those quiet moments when a handful gather where they can, speaking truth to women who had come looking for prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lydia, a seller of purple, from Thyatira—a businesswoman with means, one who worshiped God. And the Lord opened her heart. When the Lord opens a heart, neither station nor trade nor past can hold it shut.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baptized the same hour, and her whole household—faith ran through that house like water through cloth. Then she persuaded them to stay with her. How quickly the new Christian becomes the hospitable one, the one who feeds the messengers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A spirit of divination, a girl exploited for profit, bound to fortune-telling. Paul and Silas walked past daily, heading to prayer. I wonder if their hearts broke watching her, knowing whose chains she wore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Servants of the Most High God, who proclaim a way of salvation." The spirit spoke true words, yet they were meant to deceive—truth on a false tongue is still a lie. Sometimes the closest counterfeits mock the real thing most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul turned and rebuked the spirit—"In the name of Jesus Christ, come out." One sentence. One moment of boldness, and a girl's whole life changed. The name of Jesus still breaks chains that seemed permanent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The girl's masters saw their profit vanish and rage took hold. When people lose money, especially from evil-doing, they blame the righteous. Paul and Silas had freed a soul; the masters could only see a loss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "These men, being Jews, are agitating our city." Watch how the accusers twist the truth—a girl freed of a demon becomes "agitation of the city." When lies come with official robes, they can sound like law.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Customs which it is not lawful for us to accept, being Romans." The magistrates hid behind their Roman order, their Roman way. Authority often speaks not in its own voice but in the voice of law and custom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The multitude rose against them, clothes torn, rods beating—mob justice without trial. I think of how fear spreads like fire through a crowd, turning ordinary people into a fist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many stripes laid on them, then thrown into the inner prison, feet in stocks—darkness inside and out. The jailer received his orders with the weight of an empire behind them. Paul and Silas had only Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The stocks held them fast in the inner dark. Every ounce of human cleverness had conspired to silence them, lock them down, end their witness. They were exactly where power wanted them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: About midnight, Paul and Silas prayed and sang hymns—beaten, imprisoned, helpless in chains, and they sang. The prisoners listened. I've thought about this moment a thousand times; those songs were louder than any sermon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The earthquake shook the foundations; every door opened, every bond was loosened. Readers today hear an echo of what faith knows: when all chains seem permanent, the ground beneath them shifts. The Lord's mercy shows up not in courtrooms but in the dark, at midnight, for those who still sing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The jailer woke to open doors and reached for his sword—suicide seemed mercy compared to the execution Rome would demand. He had no idea what waited in that dark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Don't harm yourself, for we are all here!" Paul's voice cut through the jailer's despair. What a strange moment—the prisoner calling the jailer back to hope, to life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He fell trembling before Paul and Silas—fear gave way to wonder. Something in those two men, singing in chains, had shattered everything the jailer knew about power and dignity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" The jailer asked the question that changes lives. In that dark prison, with no escape route left, he finally asked the real question.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household." The gospel in one sentence—so simple a jailer at midnight could understand it, so true that it changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They spoke the word of the Lord to him and all his house. One conversation in a prison cell, and a whole household heard of Jesus. How often does eternity turn on one ordinary night?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The jailer washed their stripes with his own hands—the man who guarded them became their servant. Then baptized, he and his whole house. The night was full of new things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He brought them to his house and set food before them, rejoicing with his whole household. From terror to joy—a whole life turned upside down between midnight and dawn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By day, the magistrates sent word—let those men go. The rage of morning doesn't match the rage of night. Fear often flickers and dies in daylight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The jailer brought the message to Paul: go in peace. How different that sounds from "bring them out in chains." The shift was invisible but complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Paul answered: "They beat us publicly without trial—we are Romans—and now they release us in secret? No. Let them come themselves." Paul stood his ground. Sometimes meekness means refusing to let injustice hide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The magistrates heard Paul was Roman and became afraid. Authority cares for its own. The same men who beat him suddenly found reasons to be careful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They came begging and asked Paul and Silas to leave the city. Even power, caught in its own wrong, can only ask forgiveness by asking people to go. Philippi was changed but the rulers could not yet admit it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They went out of prison and entered Lydia's house. The woman who opened her heart by the riverside opened her home at the end. There they encouraged the brothers before they left. The first church at Philippi began in prayer by water and gathered strength in Lydia's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
